slides.title: Can better handoffs make an RLM more reliable?
slides.notes:
SAY: A handoff means passing a smaller task to a helper model and getting its answer back. Last time, we taught a basic Python routine. Now we study a routine using helpers and a separate reading test.

FOCUS: Can changing the RLM program make complete solutions more reliable?

CAUTION: The training and matching results are separate studies, not one learning curve.

slides.title: An RLM divides a large task into smaller steps.
slides.notes:
SAY: We want each user's count of questions asking for a location. Oslo and Kyoto qualify; Hamlet asks for a person. Helpers identify question types; Python counts: Ada one, Ben one.

WHY: The main model can inspect a file without reading it all at once. Helpers can divide work again.

CAUTION: This invented example explains the workflow, not a demonstrated ability to plan any unfamiliar task.

slides.title: We used supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to teach the main model a routine.
slides.notes:
Read the example left to right. The model sees a counting task and three helper replies. It is trained to produce code that counts the two location replies. SFT changes its learned parameters, not just its prompt.

This illustrates one step. Full examples also demonstrate asking the helper and returning the calculated answer.

Two copies started from the same model. Each learned from 72 worked interactions, using different examples and an unchanged helper.

slides.title: Both separately trained copies solved more of the 72 test tasks.
slides.notes:
The bars show confirmed successes out of all 72 attempts: 12 before SFT, 55 for one trained copy, and 53 for the other.

Six starting-model attempts and two second-copy attempts timed out after about three minutes. One further starting-model attempt ended without a verifiable final answer. These are not successful completions, and they remain in the denominator.

Both copies started from the same model. These are separate training runs, not successive stages of one run.

slides.title: We tested whether names help link each helper answer to the right statement.
slides.notes:
Read across each row: text, claim, judgment. A bike is a vehicle; blue contradicts red. The train's arrival time alone does not tell us whether it was late.

Each row is one input pair. The first two share a text; the third uses another. We do not ask the same claims about every text. The correct judgments are shown for explanation, not given to the model.

Without matching names, replies follow input order. With names, each reply repeats its pair's arbitrary name. This separate experiment uses no retraining.

slides.title: Matching names helped helpers judge many statements in one request.
slides.notes:
Qwen and Mistral are two language models. Moving right means more statements in each request. At 64, matching names raised Qwen from 44% to 83%, and Mistral from 35% to 52%.

Both formats used the same 16 sets of texts. Three Mistral replies broke the required format and were counted as wrong.

This measures helper judgments, not complete RLM solutions. Backup 6 also shows matching row numbers.

slides.title: Smaller requests were faster than large requests with matching names in this local test.
slides.notes:
SAY: All methods judged the same 768 statements. Each time covers that whole workload, not one request. Large named requests scored 85% in 91 seconds; one statement at a time scored 87% in 31 seconds.

IF ASKED: Up to four requests ran at once. Sixteen per request was faster but less accurate.

CAUTION: One-at-a-time sent about 2.5 times as much input as large named requests. This is a local tradeoff.

slides.title: Next test: let the RLM program organize helper requests and match their answers.
slides.notes:
The proposed component groups input items and matches each returned answer to its source. The main model still decides what to ask.

Today, the program matches a whole request to its response. We want it to track individual items inside that response, too. First compare fixed group sizes; choosing sizes automatically comes later.

We have not shown better complete solutions. Even perfectly matched answers can be wrong.

slides.title: We have a promising handoff result and a focused next research question.
slides.notes:
SAY: Training improved a routine; matching names improved helper reading. I recommend a focused whole-task study of the handoff procedure.

DISCUSS: Is this a worthwhile contribution? Which realistic task would make a convincing test?

STOP: This ends the ten-minute main talk. Remaining slides are optional answers to questions, not more required presentation.

slides.title: Example: the helper identifies question types, and Python adds the relevant points.
slides.notes:
SAY: Count only points attached to questions asking for a location. Ada gets four plus three, or seven. Ben gets two, not the six attached to his person question. Only Ada exceeds five: one user.

IF ASKED: The helper classifies; Python adds and compares. Wrong classifications can spoil correct arithmetic.

CAUTION: This is invented, not a copied training example. Assigned points are called weights in the experiment.

slides.title: Using the same name on a statement and its answer helped more than using different names.
slides.notes:
This asks whether adding any names helps, or whether the names must match. Both versions had names and valid formatting. Matching raised accuracy from 32.6% to 78.8%.

Answer order still told the model which statement to judge, even when the names differed.

This plot scores only the last 32 judgments in each request of 48 statements. It uses different texts from slide 6, so compare the two bars here, not across slides.

slides.title: Reward training did not improve the final-answer count in this trial.
slides.notes:
Unlike SFT, these runs learned from scores on attempted solutions. One rewarded correct final answers. The other also rewarded agreement with Python's calculation from helper replies.

The middle bar shows 55 confirmed successes. Two results are unknown, so its total could reach 57, matching the starting model.

Each run attempted 576 practice solutions before testing. These scores check final answers only; reviewing the actual calculations is unfinished.

slides.title: Training also helped with new combinations of familiar steps.
slides.notes:
First find users who asked a location question. Then count those users' number questions. The instructions supplied both steps. This tests carrying out a new combination, not inventing the plan.

There were two confirmed successes before SFT and 29 after it. Eleven earlier results and one later result are unknown. Even if all eleven earlier results succeeded, training would still be ahead.

We checked the calculation as well as the final answer.

slides.title: Misleading names can draw an answer toward the wrong input.
slides.notes:
SAY: Imagine being told to answer row seven but label it row eight. That name points to another text in the request. Accuracy was 39% with such misleading names, versus 80% with unrelated names.

IF ASKED: Order still told the model which statement to judge. Software forced the answer names.

CAUTION: Deliberate stress test, not normal use. We observed output behavior, not the model's attention.

slides.title: Both row numbers and arbitrary names helped when helpers judged many statements together.
slides.notes:
This adds matching row numbers to the comparison on slide 6. Both row numbers and arbitrary names helped.

At 64 statements, Qwen scored 44% without names, 85% with row numbers, and 83% with arbitrary names. Mistral scored 35%, 58%, and 52%, respectively.

Three Mistral replies with arbitrary names broke the required format. The difference between naming styles therefore does not measure reading ability alone.
